original_summary: In Knaresborough in 1745, Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman murdered Daniel Clarke, a shoemaker who had collected silver and jewels on credit. Clarke disappeared, and Aram lived as a respectable schoolmaster for fourteen years. In 1758, a skeleton was found near St. Robert's Cave, and Houseman's frightened reaction led to a confession and the discovery of a second skeleton at the exact burial place he described. Aram was arrested, convicted at York, and executed there on 16 August 1759.
seed_elements: Eugene Aram and Richard Houseman murder Daniel Clarke after persuading him to walk out at night to discuss how to dispose of his silver and jewels.
Aram remains apparently respectable and works as a teacher for fourteen years while Clarke is believed to have disappeared.
A labourer accidentally finds a human skeleton while digging for stone near St. Robert's Cave, leading to a coroner's inquest and suspicion of Aram and Houseman.

When asked to handle a bone, Houseman exclaims, "This is no more Daniel Clarke's bone than it is mine!" This remark makes people suspect him because they wonder how he could know that without seeing the real bones.

Houseman's confession identifies the true burial place, with Clarke's head lying a little farther to the right than the first skeleton; digging there reveals a second skeleton exactly where Houseman said it was.
Aram is arrested, gives an eloquent written defence, is quickly convicted despite it, privately confesses guilt to attending clergymen, and is executed at York on 16 August 1759.
discarded_elements: The full historical and legal detail of Aram's long written defence; retain only the contrast between his learning and the physical evidence.
The detailed account of Aram's later suicide attempt in prison.
Minor places and incidental movements connected with Aram's teaching career; keep only the fact that he taught in different towns and was traced to Lynn, Norfolk.
Extra names of officials, clergymen, witnesses, and historical figures not needed for the central case.
Technical detail about the inquest, old bones, and legal procedure beyond what is needed to explain the discovery and conviction.
conversion_plan: Write a 320-380-word, third-person, matter-of-fact historical true-crime story for A2 learners, keeping the 18th-century English setting and the real names, dates, and sequence of events. Use short sentences and explain only the essential period details, while preserving Houseman's exact exclamation, the precise second burial location, and the final execution date and place. End with one or two plain sentences that close the story without repeating the case summary.
